title: Small Business Employee Benefits: Costs, Types & Examples
summary: Small business employee benefits are the health, retirement, and lifestyle offerings a company provides beyond wages, and a few of them are required by law. This guide covers required and optional benefit types, what benefits typically cost, and how to build a package that fits a small team’s budget. You’ll leave knowing which benefits to offer first and how to expand as you grow.
body_markdown:
Benefits are how small businesses compete for people, and a small team can offer more than most owners expect.


Small businesses are increasingly finding ways to offer competitive benefit packages that go beyond traditional health, dental, and vision coverage. In addition to providing medical benefits, many employers now offer benefits such as 401(k) retirement plans, paid


family leave, flexible or remote work arrangements, fitness and wellness incentives, childcare assistance,


and student loan repayment programs. As employee benefits have become more accessible through options such as HR outsourcing, small employers have greater opportunities to build comprehensive benefit programs that may include both mandatory


employee benefits and other strategic benefit offerings designed to attract and retain talent.


## What Are Employee Benefits?


Employee benefits are forms of compensation that employers provide in addition to wages or salary, such as health insurance, retirement savings and


paid time off.


Employee benefits can include a wide range of offerings, from medical, dental, and vision coverage to retirement plans, life insurance, disability coverage, wellness programs, and flexible work arrangements. These benefits help support employees' financial, physical, and emotional well-being while also helping employers attract and retain talent.


Employee benefits generally


fall into


two categories: **required benefits** and **optional benefits** . Some benefits are mandated by federal or state law, while others are voluntarily offered by employers as part of a competitive total rewards strategy. Understanding the difference can help small business owners determine which


benefits they must provide and which benefits they may choose to offer.


## Which Employee Benefits Are Required by Law?


Many small business owners ask whether they are legally required to offer employee benefits. The answer depends on the size of the business, where it operates,


and the type of benefit being considered. While employers are


generally not required to offer


health insurance, retirement plans, dental coverage, or other voluntary benefits, several employment-related benefits and protections are required by federal law.


### Workers’ Compensation.


Most states require employers to carry workers' compensation insurance, which provides benefits to employees who sustain work-related


injuries or illnesses. Requirements and coverage rules vary by state.


### Unemployment Insurance.


Employers are


generally required to pay


federal and state unemployment taxes that fund temporary income replacement benefits for eligible workers who lose their jobs through no fault of their own.


### Social Security and Medicare Contributions.


Employers must pay and withhold payroll taxes under the Federal Insurance Contributions Act (FICA) to help fund Social Security and Medicare programs.


### Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA).


Covered employers must provide eligible employees with unpaid, job-protected and


benefits protected leave


for certain family and medical reasons. Generally,


the FMLA


applies to employers with 50 or more employees and requires eligible employees to be restored to the same or an equivalent position upon return from leave.


### Affordable Care Act (ACA) Employer Shared Responsibility.


Employers with an average of at least 50 full-time and full-time-equivalent employees are


generally required to offer


affordable medical coverage that


provides minimum value to substantially


all full-time


employees and their dependent children or potentially face an employer shared responsibility penalty.


In addition to federal requirements, some states impose additional benefit


obligations, such as temporary disability insurance, paid family and medical leave, paid sick leave, or other employee protections. Because eligibility rules vary by benefit type and jurisdiction,


employers should review applicable federal, state, and local requirements when determining which


benefits they must provide.


## Types of Employee Benefits Small Businesses Can Offer


Small business owners can consider a long list of options when it comes to employee benefits such


as medical, dental and vision insurance, retirement plans, disability and life insurance, work-life balance benefits, tuition and student loan support, lifestyle, and fringe benefits.


Here's a


look at some of those benefits:


### Medical insurance


Medical insurance is the foundation of any comprehensive benefits package. It provides employees with some protection against high medical expenses and helps them access quality healthcare. Small businesses may offer group health insurance plans that


provide employer-sponsored health coverage for eligible employees, helping businesses offer access to healthcare benefits while sharing costs with participants. These generally


are cost


effective health


insurance plans that help


support employee


well-being and strengthen their financial security.


### Dental and vision insurance


Dental and vision insurance have become essential components of employee benefit packages. They


help cover routine check-ups and procedures and promote overall


health and wellness. Including


dental insurance and vision insurance in a benefits package demonstrates a


commitment to employee well-being.


### Retirement plans


Offering retirement benefits, such as 401(k), SIMPLE IRA and


SEP IRA plans,


is a powerful tool for attracting and retaining employees. They allow


workers to save for their retirement years and help secure


their futures. Small business owners can choose to match employee contributions. Not only does this support employees' financial security, but it also aids in long-term workforce retention.


### Disability and life insurance


Disability insurance helps financially


support employees in


case of unexpected problems that hinder their ability to work. Life insurance, on the other hand, provides financial security to the beneficiaries of an employee in


the event of their


passing. Both offer peace of mind to employees, helping them secure their loved ones' futures.


### Work-life balance


In today's hybrid working world, work-life balance is a crucial consideration for all employees. Small businesses can offer flexible work schedules to help employees manage their professional and personal lives effectively. This flexibility helps reduce stress and promote overall well-being.


Including benefits like paid time off (PTO), sick days, and vacation days is routine. It’s important


to consider your industry and your employee’s workload when determining the appropriate


amount of


time for PTO.


Supporting employee well-being extends beyond physical health benefits. Employers may offer resources such as employee assistance programs


(EAPs), which provide confidential counseling, referrals, and other support services to help employees address mental health concerns, manage stress, and navigate personal or workplace challenges. By promoting mental health and emotional well-being, employers can help foster a healthier, more engaged, and more productive workforce.


### Tuition and


student loan support


Tuition reimbursement programs and student loan assistance benefits represent an


investment in employee development and financial well-being. Small businesses can empower employees to enhance their skills and knowledge by helping cover educational expenses, while also supporting those who are managing student loan debt. These benefits not only help employees pursue career growth and reduce financial stress,


but also


contribute to a more skilled workforce and strengthen the company's competitiveness. By demonstrating a


commitment to employees' long-term success, employers can foster greater loyalty, engagement, and retention.


### Lifestyle and fringe benefits


[Small businesses can further enhance their benefit offerings](https://www.trinet.com/insights/customizable-employee-benefits) with programs


that support employees' daily lives and overall well-being. Childcare assistance can


help employees manage the challenges and costs associated with caring for children, while wellness stipends may be used to support health and wellness activities such as gym memberships, fitness classes, or other well-being initiatives. Commuter benefits can help offset transportation expenses, including public transit and parking costs, making it easier and more affordable for employees to travel to and from work. These


benefits can improve employee satisfaction, support work-life balance, and contribute to a positive workplace culture.


## How much do employee benefits cost for small businesses?


Employee benefits represent a


significant investment beyond employee wages and salaries. According to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS),[benefits account for approximately 30% of total compensation costs for private industry workers, with employers spending an average of $14.01 per hour on benefits in addition to $32.60 per hour in wages and salaries](https://www.bls.gov/news.release/pdf/ecec.pdf) . While actual costs vary considerably


by employer,


benefits can represent a


substantial component of


overall workforce costs and


should be factored into overall workforce budgeting.


Several factors influence the cost of employee benefits. Headcount affects overall spending and may require


employers to comply


with certain regulatory requirements,


such as the ACA's employer shared


responsibility provisions. Plan richness also plays a


major role, as plans with lower deductibles, lower out-of-pocket costs, and broader coverage typically cost more than leaner plan designs. In addition, an employer's contribution strategy directly affects costs. Finally, costs can vary significantly by state and geographic location due to differences in insurance markets, healthcare costs, and state-mandated benefits.


Small businesses can manage benefit costs while still offering competitive coverage. One approach is to establish a


thoughtful employer benefits contribution


strategy that balances costs for


employees with budget considerations for the business. Employers may also consider high-deductible health plans (HDHPs) paired with health savings accounts


(HSAs), which can reduce premium costs while helping employees save


for eligible healthcare


expenses on a tax-advantaged basis. In addition, incorporating telehealth services can provide employees with convenient access to care and may help reduce certain healthcare expenses over time.


An effective


benefits strategy often focuses on delivering value rather than simply minimizing costs. By carefully selecting plan designs, evaluating contribution levels, and offering benefits that employees are most likely to use, small businesses can create a competitive benefits package that supports employee recruitment and retention while managing long-term expenses.

## How to build a benefits package on a small business budget


First, consider surveying employees on their needs and wants as you develop a benefits package. Then see if you can go a bit beyond that. A well-rounded


benefits package may


help improve employee satisfaction and support recruitment and


retention efforts.


Building a competitive benefits package does not have to happen all


at once. For many small businesses, a practical approach is to think in tiers,


starting with foundational benefits and expanding offerings as the organization grows. By aligning benefit investments with business goals, workforce needs, and budget realities, employers can create a package that supports recruitment and retention while remaining financially


sustainable.


A core benefits tier typically focuses on the essentials employees value most. This often includes health insurance coverage,


paid time off, and retirement savings. These foundational benefits can help


provide employees with financial security, support their well-being, and demonstrate an


employer's commitment to investing in its workforce.


As headcount and budget increase, employers may choose to add a growth tier of benefits. Additional offerings


can include programs that support financial protection, such as life or disability coverage, as well as benefits that enhance employees' day-to-day experience, such as workplace flexibility. Expanding benefits over time allows employers to respond to workforce expectations while balancing cost considerations.


More established organizations may reach a mature benefits tier, where the focus shifts from providing core protection to differentiating the employee experience. At this stage, employers may explore programs that support long-term financial, educational, and family needs, such as tuition assistance,


student loan repayment support, childcare-related benefits, or enhanced benefit plan options. These offerings can help strengthen employee engagement and support a broader range of life stages and personal goals.


Regardless of where a business falls along this spectrum, access to benefit options can be a deciding factor. Small employers purchasing coverage


on their own may encounter a


more limited selection of plans and carriers than larger organizations. Working with


a[professional employer organization (PEO) can be one way to access a broader menu of employee benefits](https://www.trinet.com/insights/compare-peo-benefits-administration) , often similar to those available at larger companies.


## Why employee benefits matter for small businesses


Employee benefits play a critical role in helping small businesses attract and retain talent. Compensation matters,


but benefits


consistently rank among the top factors candidates consider when evaluating job opportunities, particularly health insurance coverage,


retirement benefits, and paid time off. At the same time, small employers often face a competitive disadvantage compared to larger organizations, which may have greater purchasing power and access to a broader range of benefit offerings.[KFF's Employer Health Benefits Survey](https://www.kff.org/series/employer-health-benefits-survey/) has long shown meaningful differences in health insurance offer


rates between smaller and larger employers, highlighting an ongoing coverage gap that can make it more challenging for small businesses to compete for talent. For this reason, developing a thoughtful[benefits strategy](https://www.trinet.com/insights/benefits-strategies) is important and can strengthen


recruiting efforts and help position a small business as an employer of choice.


Benefits can also make financial sense from a retention perspective. Replacing an employee often involves recruiting expenses, onboarding costs, lost productivity, and the time required for a new hire to reach full effectiveness. In many cases, the cost of turnover can exceed the investment needed to provide meaningful benefits that encourage employees to stay. Rather than viewing benefits solely as an expense, small employers may benefit from


viewing them as an investment in workforce stability, employee satisfaction, and long-term business performance. By building a benefits strategy that evolves alongside the organization, employers can balance budget considerations with the need to attract, retain,


and engage a


strong workforce.

## Frequently Asked Questions


Do small businesses have to offer employee benefits?


As referenced


above, some benefits are required by law and most others are optional.


What benefits should a small business offer first?


Many employers offer health insurance, paid time off and a


retirement option, such as a 401(k) as


part of their benefits package. Additional


benefits may be considered depending on employee needs, organizational priorities, and budget considerations.


What percentage of an employee’s compensation do benefits cost?


According to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS), benefits account for approximately 30% of total compensation costs for private industry workers.


Should a small business manage benefits in-house or outsource?


[Deciding whether to outsource benefits admin](https://www.trinet.com/insights/internal-vs-outsourced-benefits-administration) depends on the business’s goals, administrative capacity


and how competitive a benefits package


the business wants to reach. A PEO is a great option to gain


access to big company benefits and administration


support.


An effective benefit


programs often start with the basics and evolve as the business grows. Rather than waiting for a perfect benefits lineup, focus on building a solid core that supports your employees now. If you need help getting started, TriNet PEO can provide tools, expertise,


and access to benefit solutions


designed for growing businesses. The right benefits strategy is the one that helps your employees thrive and your business move forward.
